distractors.c: Process-level checkpointing does not capture agent-level semantics — which questions were answered and which remain.

summary: Q106 (Cross-cutting) — The context fills with discovery output
scenario: Two hours into an exploration session, the context is dominated by verbose file listings and search results from the discovery phase. The conclusions you care about are a handful of paragraphs. You need to continue in the same session.
question: What is the appropriate tool?

options.a: /compact, having first captured the conclusions you must not lose in a scratchpad file.
options.b: Ask the model to forget the discovery output it no longer needs, freeing the space.
options.c: Restart the session with only the conclusions, since compaction always loses too much.
options.d: /compact alone, since it preserves the important information automatically and the session continues.

answerLabel: /compact, with the critical conclusions persisted first
why: /compact is the documented way to reduce context usage during extended exploration sessions filled with verbose discovery output. Because compaction is lossy, the durable findings belong in a scratchpad first (Task 5.4).

distractors.b: Asking the model to forget removes nothing: the tokens are already in the request. Taking something out of the context takes a real mechanism — compaction, API-side context editing, or a fresh session — never an instruction.
distractors.c: Restarting throws away a session you were told to continue; compaction plus a scratchpad keeps it alive and the findings intact.
distractors.d: Compaction summarises; it does not guarantee that any particular detail survives.

summary: Q107 (Cross-cutting) — A downstream agent with no room
scenario: Your synthesis agent receives, from three upstream agents, their full reasoning chains and the complete text of every source they consulted. It exhausts its context before finishing and its output degrades in the second half.
question: What should change upstream?

options.a: Have the upstream agents return structured data — key facts, citations, relevance scores — instead of raw content.
options.b: Give the synthesis agent a model with a larger context window, so everything upstream sends still fits.
options.c: Have the synthesis agent summarise each upstream contribution before incorporating it, condensing the material where it lands.
options.d: Run the synthesis agent three times, once per upstream agent, and concatenate the three partial write-ups into one report.

answerLabel: Upstream agents return structured data
why: when downstream agents have limited context budgets, the fix belongs upstream: return key facts, citations and relevance scores rather than reasoning chains and raw content (Task 5.1). The reasoning was useful to the agent that produced it; it is not what synthesis consumes.

distractors.b: Making everything fit buys headroom and leaves the ratio of signal to noise exactly where it was.
distractors.c: Makes the synthesis agent pay to read everything before condensing it — the cost you are trying to avoid.
distractors.d: Three partial syntheses concatenated is not a synthesis; cross-source connections are exactly what is lost.

summary: Q108 (Cross-cutting) — An accurate report nobody can use
scenario: Your synthesis output is factually correct and properly sourced, but readers complain it is unusable. Twelve quarters of revenue figures are described in flowing sentences, a sequence of regulatory events is presented as a bulleted list of fragments, and technical findings are buried in narrative paragraphs.
question: Where is the defect and what is the fix?

options.a: In the sourcing: readers are struggling because they cannot trace a claim back to its source quickly enough.
options.b: In the rendering: each content type should be rendered in its natural form.
options.c: In the upstream agents, which are returning content in a form the synthesis agent cannot present well.
options.d: In the volume: the report covers too much and should be split into three shorter reports.

answerLabel: A rendering defect at the synthesis step
why: when the content is correct and well sourced but hard to use, the fault is uniform rendering on output — usually everything flattened into prose, because that is the default. Different content types have different natural forms — tables for figures, prose for events and context, structured lists for technical findings — and the synthesis agent should be instructed accordingly (Task 5.6).

distractors.a: Tracing claims is not the complaint: the sourcing is described as sound, and readers are stuck on the presentation.
distractors.c: The scenario states the content is correct and sourced; the upstream agents did their job.
distractors.d: Splitting an unreadable report produces three unreadable reports.

summary: Q109 (Cross-cutting) — Reducing human review safely (Select the 2 correct answers.)
scenario: Your extraction system currently sends every document to human review. You want to reduce that load without letting error rates rise unnoticed.
question: Which two measures belong in the design?

options.a: Set the review threshold at the aggregate accuracy figure already reported by the pipeline.
options.b: Have the model output field-level confidence scores and calibrate the review threshold against a labelled validation set.
options.c: Review only the document types that historically produced the most complaints.
options.d: Maintain ongoing stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to measure real error rates and detect novel error patterns.
options.e: Have the model self-rate each extraction from 1 to 10 and review anything below 8.

answerLabel: calibrated field-level confidence, plus ongoing stratified sampling
why: the two halves of Task 5.5. Field-level confidence calibrated on labelled data tells you where to send the reviewers you have; stratified sampling of the extractions you stopped reviewing tells you whether the automation is still safe, and surfaces error patterns nobody anticipated. One routes, the other monitors — dropping either leaves the design incomplete.

distractors.a: An aggregate figure is exactly what conceals a badly performing segment; it is not a threshold.
distractors.e: Uncalibrated self-rating on an arbitrary scale — the model is confident where it is wrong.
distractors.c: Complaint history is a lagging and biased signal; the errors nobody complained about are the ones you most need to find.

summary: Q110 (Cross-cutting) — Reliable escalation triggers (Select the 2 correct answers.)
scenario: You are writing the escalation section of a support agent's system prompt and must choose which signals genuinely warrant handing off to a human.
question: Which two are reliable escalation triggers?

options.a: The customer's request falls into a gap where policy is silent or ambiguous.
options.b: The conversation has exceeded fifty turns and the context window is filling up.
options.c: The customer's message registers strong negative sentiment.
options.d: The agent has made no meaningful progress after a reasonable number of attempts.
options.e: The agent's self-reported confidence for the case falls below 7 out of 10.

answerLabel: the policy gap, and the absence of meaningful progress
why: the reliable triggers are an explicit request for a human, a policy exception or gap, and an inability to make meaningful progress. The policy gap and the stalled case are two of those three (Task 5.2).

distractors.c: Sentiment does not correlate with case complexity — a furious customer may have a trivial problem.
distractors.e: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and is high precisely on the hard cases.
distractors.b: A filling context window is a technical constraint with technical remedies (case facts, compaction), not a business reason to involve a human.

summary: Q111 (Cross-cutting) — Passing context to a subagent (Select the 2 correct answers.)
scenario: Your coordinator delegates to a synthesis subagent that must combine the outputs of a web search agent and a document analysis agent, while preserving source attribution.
question: Which two practices are correct?

options.a: Give the subagent read access to the other subagents' sessions so it can consult them as needed.
options.b: Pass the coordinator's entire transcript, so nothing the subagent might need can be missing.
options.c: Include the complete findings from the prior agents directly in the subagent's prompt.
options.d: Rely on the subagent inheriting the coordinator's conversation history automatically, as a spawned process would.
options.e: Use a structured format that separates content from metadata — source URLs, document names, page numbers.

answerLabel: the prior findings passed explicitly in the prompt, in a content/metadata structure
why: subagents have isolated context, so everything they need is provided explicitly in the prompt; and separating content from metadata is what preserves attribution through the handoff (Task 1.3).

distractors.d: A subagent is not a spawned process that inherits its parent's state: there is no automatic inheritance, and this is the single most common misconception about subagents.
distractors.b: The full transcript floods the subagent's context with material irrelevant to its task; "complete findings" is not "everything that happened".
distractors.a: Cross-session access breaks both the isolation of subagents and the hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator.

summary: Q112 (Cross-cutting) — Guarantees versus best effort (Select the 2 correct answers.)
scenario: Two requirements must hold every single time: identity must be verified before any refund is processed, and no refund above $500 may be issued by the agent.
question: Which two mechanisms provide a deterministic guarantee?

options.a: Few-shot examples showing the agent verifying identity first and escalating a $750 refund.
options.b: A programmatic prerequisite that blocks process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
options.c: A hook that intercepts the outgoing refund call, blocks amounts above $500, and redirects to escalation.
options.d: A system prompt stating that verification is mandatory and that refunds above $500 must be escalated.
options.e: A nightly audit that flags any refund issued without a prior verification call.

answerLabel: the prerequisite gate, and the tool-call interception hook
why: both are enforcement in code, evaluated on the actual call and its actual arguments. Prerequisite gates and tool-call interception hooks are the two mechanisms the guide names for deterministic compliance (Tasks 1.4 and 1.5).

distractors.a: Demonstrations shape behaviour probabilistically: an agent that has been shown the right sequence can still depart from it, and no example is evaluated against the arguments of the call actually being made.
distractors.d: An instruction shapes behaviour probabilistically too. It lowers the failure rate without making it zero, and "every single time" is the stated requirement.
distractors.e: Detects violations after the money has moved. Detection is not prevention.
